implementation_notes: Foundation ships the pattern: Measurement<UnitType> is a value type pairing a magnitude with a Unit, and every Measurement whose UnitType is a Dimension gains converted(to:) plus the + and - operators built on the unit's UnitConverter, with 21 predefined Unit subclasses (UnitLength, UnitMass, UnitDuration, UnitTemperature, ...). Custom units are cheap - extend the dimension class with a static property pairing a symbol and a UnitConverterLinear coefficient - which is exactly Fowler's Conversion Ratio object embedded in the unit, and UnitConverterReciprocal covers non-linear fuel-economy-style conversions. What Foundation does not provide is derived dimensions: a Measurement<UnitLength> divided by a Measurement<UnitDuration> does not compile until you write the operator yourself, so compound quantities need your own operators or a hand-written struct per dimension.
pitfalls: When the operand units differ, + and - convert to the Dimension's base unit, so the result's unit is not the left operand's - surprising in formatted output.
Measurement is generic over the unit class, so erasing to any Dimension loses converted(to:) unless you cast back; typealiases such as Length = Measurement<UnitLength> keep signatures readable.
UnitConverterLinear coefficients are Double, so exact values (inches to centimetres) accumulate floating-point error through chained conversions - round only at presentation.

variants.name: Hand-written struct per dimension
variants.idiom_name: struct Length with a canonical stored unit + static factories
variants.implementation_notes: When the unit set is closed and Foundation's 21 dimensions are the wrong shape, a struct per dimension with a private stored base-unit value, static factories (Length.kilometers(3)) and conversion accessors gives the same value semantics with your own vocabulary - Swift value types, Equatable/Hashable synthesis and no reference sharing. It is the classic value object again, and it is only worth it while the unit list is small; the conversion table must then be maintained by hand.
pitfalls: A memberwise or public initializer lets callers attach a raw Double to the wrong unit; keep the canonical initializer private and expose named factories.
Equatable synthesis compares the stored representation, so equality is unit-insensitive only because everything is normalised - keep that invariant or the semantics change silently.
Hand-copied factors drift from the ones used by servers or databases; generate or test them against a single table.
